title: Communication
summary: Make a chart that explains its finding to others. Add a clear title, labels and readable axes. Use patchwork to place a second chart beside it.

steps.title: Setup: library(tidyverse), library(ggrepel), library(patchwork)

runs.purpose: load the tidyverse, which includes ggplot2
load ggrepel, whose labels move out of each other's way
load patchwork, which puts charts side by side

steps.explain: ggplot2 comes with the tidyverse. ggrepel adds labels that don't overlap, and patchwork combines charts with `+`. The `scales` package, installed with ggplot2, formats axis labels; its functions are called as `scales::` without attaching it.

steps.title: A chart for exploring

runs.code:
by_hour <- read_csv("data/trips.csv") |>
  filter(wday(started_at, week_start = 1) <= 5) |>
  count(hour = hour(started_at), member_type)
alternatives: by_hour = read_csv('data/trips.csv', show_col_types = FALSE) |> filter(!wday(started_at, label = TRUE) %in% c('Sat', 'Sun')) |> count(hour = hour(started_at), member_type)
runs.purpose: count the weekday trips that started in each hour, for members and casual riders, as `by_hour`
runs.task: Read `data/trips.csv`, keep Monday to Friday (`wday(started_at, week_start = 1) <= 5`), and count the trips by `hour` (`hour(started_at)`) and `member_type`. Store the result in `by_hour`.

runs.code:
base <- ggplot(by_hour, aes(x = hour, y = n, colour = member_type)) +
  geom_line()
alternatives: base = ggplot(by_hour, aes(hour, n, colour = member_type)) + geom_line()
runs.purpose: make a line chart of trips by hour, one line per member type, and keep it as `base`
runs.task: Make a line chart of `n` against `hour` for `by_hour`, coloured by `member_type`. Store it in `base` without printing it.

steps.explain:
A ggplot is an object like any other: `base <- …` keeps the chart without drawing it, and printing `base` draws it. Each step of this lesson adds to the last step's chart and keeps the result under a new name, so a step can be run again without adding anything twice.

`base` is fine for exploring {n_weekday} weekday trips, but someone else would have to work out what `n` is, which hour is which, and what the chart is telling them.

steps.title: Say what it shows: labs()

runs.code:
labelled <- base +
  labs(
    title = "Members ride at the rush hours, casual riders all afternoon",
    subtitle = "Trips started in each hour of a weekday, 2025",
    x = "Hour of the day",
    y = "Trips",
    colour = "Rider",
    caption = "Data: Larkhaven Bikes"
  )
alternatives: labelled = base + labs(title = 'Members ride at the rush hours, casual riders all afternoon', subtitle = 'Trips started in each hour of a weekday, 2025', x = 'Hour of the day', y = 'Trips', colour = 'Rider', caption = 'Data: Larkhaven Bikes')
runs.purpose: add a title that states the finding, a subtitle, a caption and plain axis and legend titles, as `labelled`
runs.task: Add labels to `base` with `labs()`. Set the title to "Members ride at the rush hours, casual riders all afternoon". Set the subtitle to "Trips started in each hour of a weekday, 2025". Name the x and y axes "Hour of the day" and "Trips". Name the colour legend "Rider" with `colour =` and add the caption "Data: Larkhaven Bikes". Store the result in `labelled`.

steps.explain:
`labs()` replaces the variable names ggplot2 used as titles. The title says what the chart shows rather than what it is: a reader should get the point before looking at the lines.

The subtitle adds what was counted, the caption says where the data came from, and `colour =` names the legend after the aesthetic it explains.

steps.title: Point at the peaks: geom_label_repel()

runs.code:
peaks <- by_hour |>
  slice_max(n, by = member_type) |>
  mutate(label = paste0(scales::comma(n), " trips at ", hour, ":00"))
alternatives: peaks = by_hour |> group_by(member_type) |> slice_max(n) |> ungroup() |> mutate(label = paste0(scales::comma(n), ' trips at ', hour, ':00'))
runs.purpose: find each rider type's busiest hour and write a label for it, as `peaks`
runs.task: Keep the busiest hour for each `member_type` with `slice_max()`. Add `label`, such as "9,672 trips at 8:00", using `paste0()` and `scales::comma(n)`. Store the result in `peaks`.

runs.code:
annotated <- labelled +
  geom_point(data = peaks) +
  geom_label_repel(
    aes(label = label),
    data = peaks,
    seed = 1,
    show.legend = FALSE
  )
alternatives: annotated = labelled + geom_point(data = peaks) + geom_label_repel(data = peaks, mapping = aes(label = label), seed = 1, show.legend = FALSE)
runs.purpose: mark each peak with a point and a label, as `annotated`
runs.task: Add a point at each `peaks` row to `labelled` with `geom_point(data = peaks)`. Add a label from `label` with `geom_label_repel()`, `seed = 1` and `show.legend = FALSE`. Store the result in `annotated`.

steps.explain:
A layer can draw a different data frame from the chart's: `data = peaks` gives these two layers just the two busiest hours, which inherit the chart's mappings, colour included. The labels state the numbers a reader would otherwise estimate from the axis: {member_peak} for members, {casual_peak} for casual riders.

`geom_label_repel()` moves each label away from the data and from the other labels; `seed = 1` makes it place them the same way every time, and `show.legend = FALSE` keeps a letter out of the legend.

steps.title: Readable axes: scales

runs.code:
scaled <- annotated +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 3),
    labels = scales::label_number(suffix = ":00")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())
alternatives: scaled = annotated + scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24), labels = scales::label_number(suffix = ':00')) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma())
runs.purpose: mark the hours every three hours, written as times, and put commas in the trip counts, as `scaled`
runs.task: Add an x scale to `annotated` with breaks every 3 hours from 0 to 24 (`seq(0, 24, by = 3)`). Format those labels with `scales::label_number(suffix = ":00")`. Format the y labels with `scales::label_comma()`. Store the result in `scaled`.

steps.explain:
Every aesthetic has a scale, which ggplot2 adds with defaults: here, x breaks every 5 hours and plain numbers. `breaks` chooses where the ticks go, every 3 hours, and `labels` how they read: `scales::label_number(suffix = ":00")` turns 18 into 18:00, and `scales::label_comma()` writes 9,000 rather than 9000.

The `scales` package has a `label_` function for most formats: percentages, money, dates.

steps.title: A theme and the legend: theme()

runs.purpose: use a plainer theme and move the legend above the chart, as `polished`
runs.task: Add `theme_minimal()` to `scaled`, then move the legend to the top with `theme(legend.position = "top")`. Store the result in `polished`.

steps.explain:
A theme controls everything not drawn from the data: background, grid lines, fonts, the legend's place. `theme_minimal()` drops the grey background, so the lines stand out. `theme()` then changes single elements: with the legend at the top, the lines get the chart's full width.

A complete theme such as `theme_minimal()` resets every element, so it comes before the changes made with `theme()`.

steps.title: Side by side: patchwork

runs.code:
totals <- ggplot(by_hour, aes(x = member_type, y = n, fill = member_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Weekday trips") +
  theme_minimal()
alternatives: totals = ggplot(by_hour, aes(member_type, n, fill = member_type)) + geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) + labs(x = NULL, y = 'Weekday trips') + theme_minimal()
runs.purpose: make a bar chart of each rider type's total weekday trips, as `totals`
runs.task: Make a bar chart of total `n` by `member_type` in `by_hour`, filled by `member_type`. Use `geom_col(show.legend = FALSE)` and comma y labels. Set the y title to "Weekday trips", leave the x title empty, and add `theme_minimal()`. Store it in `totals`.

runs.purpose: put the two charts side by side, the line chart three times as wide
runs.task: Put `polished` and `totals` side by side with `+`, the first three times as wide, with `plot_layout(widths = c(3, 1))`.

steps.explain:
With patchwork attached, `+` between two charts puts them side by side (`/` would stack them), and `plot_layout()` sets their widths. The bar chart answers the question the lines raise: how many trips each kind of rider makes in all.

`geom_col()` stacks each rider type's 24 hourly counts into one bar: {member_total} weekday trips by members and {casual_total} by casual riders. Two charts that share a style, colours included, read as one figure.
